title: signing secrets are generated with the non-cryptographic random module
what_is_wrong: The secret is built from random.choice over an alphabet, and random is a Mersenne Twister PRNG whose state can be reconstructed from observed output, so an attacker who sees a few secrets can predict others and forge signatures.

title: signature comparison is a plain == instead of a constant-time compare
what_is_wrong: verify returns expected == signature, and Python's string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking digest prefix information through timing to a caller that can supply candidate signatures.

title: the signature does not cover the timestamp it is sent with
what_is_wrong: sign returns a timestamp and an HMAC computed only over the serialized payload, so the X-Acme-Timestamp header is unauthenticated and can be rewritten by a replayer without invalidating the signature.

title: the signed bytes are not the bytes that are transmitted
what_is_wrong: sign hashes json.dumps(payload, sort_keys=True) while client.post(json=...) re-serializes the payload with httpx's own encoder (different key order and separators), so the receiver recomputing the HMAC over the raw body it received gets a different digest.

title: verify recomputes a fresh timestamp and ignores the one on the request
what_is_wrong: verify calls sign again, discarding the returned timestamp and never comparing it to the request's, so the helper we publish as the reference implementation cannot enforce the replay window the docs require.

title: the status CHECK constraint does not allow the terminal status the code writes
what_is_wrong: The CHECK permits only 'pending', 'in_flight', 'delivered', 'failed', while _finish writes 'failed_permanent', so every permanently failed delivery raises a constraint violation instead of being recorded.

title: the unique index on event_id alone allows only one delivery row per event
what_is_wrong: UNIQUE (event_id) makes a second insert for the same event_id fail, so an org with two subscribed endpoints cannot have both deliveries enqueued and the whole add_all aborts.

title: time.sleep blocks the event loop inside an async coroutine
what_is_wrong: deliver awaits httpx but then calls the synchronous time.sleep(delay) for backoff, which halts the entire event loop so every other delivery in the asyncio.gather and the worker itself stall for up to 16 seconds per retry.

title: ORM rows are returned after their session has closed
what_is_wrong: _claim_batch returns the query results from inside the with session_scope() block, so by the time deliver reads row.payload, row.attempts or row.id the instances are detached and expired and attribute access raises DetachedInstanceError.

title: the endpoint object is used outside the session that loaded it
what_is_wrong: endpoint = session.get(...) is assigned inside the with block and then endpoint.signing_secret and endpoint.url are read after the session closed, so the attribute load fires against a dead session.

title: the deliveries endpoint never checks that the endpoint belongs to the caller's org
what_is_wrong: The query filters only on endpoint_id taken from the path, so any authenticated user can enumerate delivery history, event ids and event types for any other organization's endpoints.

title: to_dict exposes the signing secret on every read path
what_is_wrong: to_dict includes signing_secret, and list_webhook_endpoints returns it for all endpoints, so the shared HMAC key is handed out on every GET rather than only at creation.

title: registered URLs are not restricted to public hosts, giving SSRF
what_is_wrong: The only check is a scheme prefix and a non-empty netloc, so a user can register http://127.0.0.1/ or http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data and have the worker POST to internal services from inside the network.

title: follow_redirects=True lets a receiver bounce the signed payload to another host
what_is_wrong: The AsyncClient is constructed with follow_redirects=True, so a 302 from a customer endpoint causes httpx to re-send the payload and the signature headers to an arbitrary destination the user never registered.

title: the distributed lock is acquired with a non-atomic get-then-set
what_is_wrong: _acquire_lock reads LOCK_KEY, then sets it, so two workers that both read a missing key both proceed and dispatch the same batch, duplicating every delivery.

title: set and expire are separate commands so a crash leaves the lock permanent
what_is_wrong: The TTL is applied by a second expire call after set, and a process that dies between them leaves LOCK_KEY with no expiry, permanently wedging every worker.

title: the lock is deleted unconditionally without checking ownership
what_is_wrong: The finally block calls redis_client.delete(LOCK_KEY) with no fencing value, so a worker whose 60-second lock already expired deletes the lock now held by a different worker.

title: the 60-second lock TTL is shorter than a batch can take
what_is_wrong: The lock expires after 60 seconds while a batch of up to 100 deliveries with a 30-second timeout and four backoff sleeps can run for minutes, so a second worker starts claiming and delivering while the first is still in flight.

title: rows are claimed without row-level locking
what_is_wrong: The claim is a plain SELECT followed by an in-Python status assignment with no FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so two concurrent transactions can select and claim the same pending rows.

title: a delivery left in in_flight is never recovered
what_is_wrong: status is set to in_flight at claim time and only rewritten by _finish, so any worker crash, cancellation or unhandled exception strands the row in in_flight where no query will ever pick it up again.

title: attempts is only persisted at a terminal state so the retry cap is not durable
what_is_wrong: row.attempts is written solely by _finish on success or permanent failure, so a delivery that fails four times and then crashes reappears with attempts still 0 and gets a fresh full quota of attempts.

title: all retries happen inside one in-process loop, so next_attempt_at is never used
what_is_wrong: The while loop performs up to MAX_ATTEMPTS attempts in a single pass and never resets the row to pending with a future next_attempt_at, so the scheduled-retry column and the pending-queue design are dead and no retry survives a restart.

title: 4xx responses are retried although the code only special-cases 2xx
what_is_wrong: The success branch tests 200 <= status < 300 and everything else falls through to the retry path, so a 400 or 404 is retried five times instead of being treated as permanent.

title: the backoff has no jitter
what_is_wrong: backoff_for returns exactly BASE_DELAY_SECONDS ** attempt seconds, so all deliveries that failed in the same batch retry in lockstep and hammer the receiver in synchronized waves.

title: only httpx.HTTPError is caught, so any other exception aborts the whole batch
what_is_wrong: Exceptions from _finish, from session_scope, or a None endpoint escape deliver into asyncio.gather, which is called without return_exceptions=True, so one bad delivery cancels the sibling coroutines and leaves them in in_flight.

title: the loaded endpoint is not checked for None
what_is_wrong: session.get returns None when the endpoint row was deleted, and endpoint.signing_secret then raises AttributeError inside the retry loop, which is not an HTTPError and so is not caught.

title: the delivery row is not checked for None before being mutated
what_is_wrong: _finish assigns row.status immediately after session.get, so a delivery whose row was removed by a cascading endpoint delete raises AttributeError and takes down the gather.

title: the outbound signature and headers are written to the application log
what_is_wrong: log.info("POST %s headers=%s", ...) logs the full header dict including X-Acme-Signature, putting an authentication credential derived from the shared secret into logs that get shipped and indexed.

title: the entire response body is persisted with no size bound
what_is_wrong: _finish stores response.text and the f-string detail straight into response_body TEXT, so a receiver returning a multi-megabyte body writes it verbatim into the database on every attempt.

title: next_attempt_at is written as a naive datetime while the claim query compares against an aware one
what_is_wrong: enqueue_for_event uses datetime.utcnow() (naive) whereas _claim_batch filters with datetime.now(timezone.utc), so the comparison mixes naive and aware values against a timezone-aware column.

title: an async function does entirely blocking database work
what_is_wrong: enqueue_for_event, _claim_batch and _finish are synchronous SQLAlchemy calls invoked from coroutines with no thread offload, so every database round trip blocks the event loop that is supposed to be running deliveries concurrently.

title: an exception from _claim_batch kills the worker permanently
what_is_wrong: The try block has only a finally, so a transient database error propagates out of the while loop and terminates run_worker with no restart, silently stopping all webhook delivery.

title: batch may be unbound when it is tested
what_is_wrong: if not batch runs after the try/finally, and the name is only assigned inside the try, so a failure in _claim_batch would reach the test with batch undefined were the exception ever suppressed.

title: webhook enqueue failures are swallowed, so events are silently never delivered
what_is_wrong: The enqueue call is wrapped in except Exception with only a log.warning, and it runs after the event transaction has already committed, so a database blip drops the webhook for that event with no outbox row and no retry.

title: the swallowed exception is logged without a traceback
what_is_wrong: log.warning formats only str(exc) with no exc_info, so the stack that would identify why enqueue failed is discarded.

title: a hardcoded three-type allowlist silently overrides per-endpoint subscriptions
what_is_wrong: Only invoice.paid, invoice.payment_failed and subscription.updated ever reach enqueue_for_event, so an endpoint that registered any other event type, or an empty list meaning all types, receives nothing and gets no error.

title: the URL scheme check accepts plaintext http and bogus schemes
what_is_wrong: not parsed.scheme.startswith("http") passes for http, and also for httpfoo or httpx, so non-TLS and nonsense schemes are stored and later handed to httpx.

title: event_types is stored without validating the names against the emitted set
what_is_wrong: Any string list is accepted and persisted, so a typo such as invoice.payed silently subscribes the endpoint to nothing and the user gets a 201 with no indication.

title: the feature flag added by the migration is never read
what_is_wrong: The migration adds webhooks_enabled defaulting to FALSE, but neither the routes nor the dispatcher nor the delivery worker consults it, so webhooks are live for every org and the column is inert.

title: the shared HMAC secret is stored in plaintext
what_is_wrong: signing_secret is a plain TEXT column with no encryption or wrapping, so any database dump, replica or read-only analytics role yields every customer's webhook signing key.

title: the migration uses TIMESTAMP while the models declare timezone-aware columns
what_is_wrong: created_at, updated_at and next_attempt_at are TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE in SQL but DateTime(timezone=True) in models.py, so the offset written by aware Python datetimes is dropped by the database.

title: there is no index supporting the queries the code actually issues
what_is_wrong: Only status and event_id are indexed, while _claim_batch filters status and orders by next_attempt_at and list_deliveries filters endpoint_id ordering by created_at, so both do sorts over unindexed columns.

title: the migration has no rollback path
what_is_wrong: The file contains only forward DDL inside BEGIN/COMMIT with no corresponding down migration, so the two tables and the organizations column cannot be reverted by the migration tool.

title: nothing prevents unlimited duplicate endpoints per org
what_is_wrong: There is no unique constraint on (org_id, url) and no count limit, so the same URL can be registered repeatedly and each copy multiplies the deliveries for every event.

title: the model narrows event_type to 100 characters while the migration allows unbounded TEXT
what_is_wrong: Column(String(100)) and TEXT disagree, so a value the database accepts fails the model's own length expectation depending on which path writes it.

title: the STATUSES tuple is declared but never enforced anywhere
what_is_wrong: STATUSES lists the four legal values yet no column, validator or check references it, so it documents nothing the code actually applies and drifts from the migration's CHECK.

title: updated_at has a creation default but no onupdate
what_is_wrong: The column defaults to _now at insert with no onupdate=_now, so any write that is not routed through _finish leaves updated_at showing the insert time.

title: created_at and updated_at are nullable in the model but NOT NULL in the migration
what_is_wrong: Neither column declares nullable=False, so an ORM insert that bypasses the Python-side default sends NULL and is rejected by the database rather than by validation.

title: nothing in the delivered request identifies the event
what_is_wrong: The request body is the raw event payload and the headers carry only a timestamp and signature, so a receiver has no event id or event type to deduplicate on despite delivery being at-least-once.

title: the limit parameter has a lower bound but no upper bound
what_is_wrong: Query(50, ge=1) permits limit=1000000, so a single request can pull an unbounded number of delivery rows and their serialization into memory.

title: the endpoint listing is unpaginated
what_is_wrong: The query has no limit or offset and returns every endpoint for the org in one response, so the payload grows without bound as endpoints accumulate.

title: the request model accepts arbitrary extra fields and an unbounded url
what_is_wrong: EndpointIn declares url as a bare str with no length limit and no extra="forbid", so unknown keys are ignored silently and a megabyte-long string is stored in the TEXT column.

title: there is no way to deactivate, delete or rotate an endpoint
what_is_wrong: active is hardcoded True at creation and only POST and GET routes exist, so a customer whose secret leaks or whose URL changes has no API path to fix it.

title: deliveries are fanned out with no per-endpoint concurrency limit
what_is_wrong: asyncio.gather is applied to the whole batch of up to 100 rows at once, so several deliveries destined for one endpoint hit it simultaneously.

title: SECRET_BYTES counts characters, not bytes
what_is_wrong: new_signing_secret picks SECRET_BYTES characters from a 62-symbol alphabet, so the constant's name misstates the entropy and any future switch to token_bytes silently changes the secret length.

title: the documented https-only restriction is not implemented
what_is_wrong: The doc promises https-only registration while create_webhook_endpoint accepts any scheme beginning with http, so customers are told their payloads travel over TLS when they may not.

file: docs/webhooks.md — "it cannot be read back afterwards"
title: the doc claims the signing secret is write-once
what_is_wrong: list_webhook_endpoints returns to_dict for every endpoint including signing_secret, so the secret is readable on demand contrary to the stated contract.

title: the documented signing input does not match the code
what_is_wrong: The doc says the HMAC covers "{timestamp}.{raw_request_body}" whereas sign hashes only a re-serialized payload, so any customer implementing verification from the doc rejects every request.

file: docs/webhooks.md — "An empty event_types subscribes the endpoint to every event type"
title: the documented wildcard subscription is limited to three hardcoded types
what_is_wrong: dispatch only forwards events whose type is in WEBHOOK_EVENT_TYPES, so an empty event_types receives three types rather than every event emitted.

file: docs/webhooks.md — "a 4xx is permanent and we stop immediately"
title: the documented 4xx behaviour is the opposite of the code
what_is_wrong: deliver retries every non-2xx response up to MAX_ATTEMPTS, so a 400 or 410 is retried four more times instead of stopping.

title: jitter is documented but not implemented
what_is_wrong: backoff_for is a pure power of two with no randomisation, so the described jitter does not exist.

file: docs/webhooks.md — "reject requests whose timestamp is more than five minutes old"
title: our own verify helper does not do what the doc asks receivers to do
what_is_wrong: The doc instructs a five-minute freshness check and constant-time comparison, while verify ignores the timestamp entirely and uses ==, so the shipped reference contradicts the published guidance.

title: the doc tells receivers to dedupe on a field they are never sent
what_is_wrong: Nothing in the body or the headers carries event_id, so the instruction cannot be followed.

file: docs/webhooks.md — "an endpoint belonging to your organization"
title: the doc asserts an ownership scope the handler does not enforce
what_is_wrong: list_deliveries filters only on the path endpoint_id, so the documented per-organization scoping is absent.

title: the test never verifies the signature against the transmitted body
what_is_wrong: It asserts only that the header starts with sha256= and is the right length, so the mismatch between the signed serialization and the body httpx actually sends passes the test that claims to cover the signed payload.

title: the round-trip test is tautological
what_is_wrong: verify calls sign internally, so the assertion holds for any deterministic MAC regardless of canonicalization, timestamp binding or header format, and cannot fail for the reasons it appears to guard.

title: the test asserts a constant against a literal instead of behaviour
what_is_wrong: assert MAX_ATTEMPTS == 5 exercises no retry code, so the attempt cap could be ignored entirely by deliver and the test would stay green.

title: the retry loop, batch claim, lock and enqueue paths have no tests at all
what_is_wrong: Only signing helpers, backoff_for and send_once are covered, leaving deliver, _claim_batch, _acquire_lock, _finish, enqueue_for_event and run_worker — where the concurrency and durability bugs live — entirely unexercised.

title: the secret test checks shape only and passes for a predictable generator
what_is_wrong: It asserts the prefix and total length, so swapping a CSPRNG for random.choice, or even a constant per-process seed, leaves the test green.

title: the backoff test pins the undocumented no-jitter behaviour and skips the boundary attempts
what_is_wrong: The parametrization covers attempts 1 to 4 with exact equality, which both codifies the absence of the documented jitter and never exercises attempt 0 or the MAX_ATTEMPTS boundary.

title: hand-rolled fakes of the ORM models hide the detached-instance and missing-row failures
what_is_wrong: The fakes expose plain class attributes that always resolve, so send_once is tested against objects that can never be expired, detached, or None the way real WebhookEndpoint and WebhookDelivery rows are.

title: fake state lives on the class rather than an instance
what_is_wrong: attempts, id and payload are class attributes, so any test that mutated a fake would leak that mutation into every other test through shared state.
